Exploration from a Primal-Dual Lens: Value-Incentivized Actor-Critic Methods for Sample-Efficient Online RL

Tong Yang ††thanks: Carnegie Mellon University; Emails: {tongyang,yuejiec}@andrew.cmu.edu. Affiliation: CMU    Bo Dai ††thanks: Georgia Institute of Technology; Email: bodai@cc.gatech.edu. Affiliation: Georgia Tech    Lin Xiao ††thanks: Fundamental AI Research, Meta; Email: {linx,ychi}@meta.com. Affiliation: Meta    Yuejie Chi Affiliation: Meta & CMU
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Online reinforcement learning (RL) with complex function approximations such as transformers and deep neural networks plays a significant role in the modern practice of artificial intelligence. Despite its popularity and importance, balancing the fundamental trade-off between exploration and exploitation remains a long-standing challenge; in particular, we are still in lack of efficient and practical schemes that are backed by theoretical performance guarantees. Motivated by recent developments in exploration via optimistic regularization, this paper provides an interpretation of the principle of optimism through the lens of primal-dual optimization. From this fresh perspective, we set forth a new value-incentivized actor-critic (VAC) method, which optimizes a single easy-to-optimize objective integrating exploration and exploitation — it promotes state-action and policy estimates that are both consistent with collected data transitions and result in higher value functions. Theoretically, the proposed VAC method has near-optimal regret guarantees under linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) in both finite-horizon and infinite-horizon settings, which can be extended to the general function approximation setting under appropriate assumptions.

Keywords: actor-critic methods, primal-dual, exploration by regularization, function approximation

1 Introduction

In online reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton et al., 1998), an agent learns to update their policy in an adaptive manner while interacting with an unknown environment to maximize long-term cumulative rewards. In conjunction with complex function approximation such as large neural networks and foundation models to reduce dimensionality, online RL has achieved remarkable performance in a wide variety of applications such as game playing (Silver et al., 2017), control (Mnih et al., 2015), language model post-training (OpenAI, 2023; Team et al., 2023) and reasoning (Guo et al., 2025), and many others.

Despite its popularity, advancing beyond current successes is severely bottlenecked by the cost and constraints associated with data collection. While simulators can subsidize data acquisition in certain domains, many real-world applications—such as clinical trials, recommendation systems and autonomous driving—operate under conditions where gathering interaction data is expensive, time-consuming or potentially risky. In these high-stake scenarios, managing the fundamental yet delicate trade-off between exploration (gathering new information about the environment) and exploitation (leveraging existing knowledge to maximize rewards) requires paramount care. Naive exploration schemes, such as the ϵ\epsilon-greedy method, are known to be sample-inefficient as they explore randomly without strategic information gathering (Dann et al., 2022). Arguably, it is still an open challenge to develop practical online RL algorithms that come with provable sample-efficiency guarantees, especially in the presence of function approximation.

Addressing this limitation, significant research attempts have been made to develop statistically efficient approaches, often guided by the principle of optimism in the face of uncertainty (Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020). Prominent approaches include constructing optimistic estimates with data-driven confidence sets (Auer et al., 2008; Agarwal et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025; Foster et al., 2021), as well as employing Bayesian methods like Thompson sampling (Russo et al., 2018) and its optimistic variants (Agrawal and Jia, 2017; Zhang, 2022). While appealing theoretically, translating them into practical algorithms compatible with general function approximators often proves difficult. Many such theoretically-grounded approaches either suffer from prohibitive computational complexity or exhibit underwhelming empirical performance when scaled to complex problems.

Recently, Liu et al. (2024) introduced an intriguing framework termed Maximize to Explore (MEX) for online RL, which optimizes a single objective function over the state-action value function (i.e., QQ-function), elegantly unifying estimation, planning and exploration in one framework. In addition, MEX comes with appealing sub-linear regret guarantees under function approximation. However, the practical optimization of the MEX objective presents significant challenges due to its inherent bi-level structure. Specifically, it incorporates the optimal value function derived from the target QQ-function as a regularizer (Kumar and Becker, 1982), which is not directly amenable to first-order optimization toolkits. As a result, nontrivial modifications are introduced in the said implementation of MEX, making it challenging to ablate the benefit of the MEX framework. This practical hurdle raises a crucial question:

Can we design a sample-efficient model-free online RL algorithm that optimizes a unifying objective function, but without resorting to complex bilevel optimization?

1.1 Our contribution

In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative, introducing a novel actor-critic method that achieves near-optimal regret guarantees by optimizing a single non-bilevel objective. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    Incentivizing exploration from the primal-dual perspective. We start by offering a new interpretation of MEX, where optimistic regularization—central to MEX—arises naturally from a Lagrangian formulation within a primal-dual optimization perspective (Dai et al., 2018; Nachum and Dai, 2020). Specifically, we demonstrate that the seemingly complex MEX objective function can be derived as the regularized Lagrangian of a canonical value maximization problem, subject to the constraint that the QQ-function satisfies the Bellman optimality equation. This viewpoint allows deeper understanding of the structure of the MEX objective and its exploration mechanism.

  • •

    VAC: Value-incentivized actor-critic method. Motivated by this Lagrangian interpretation, we develop the value-incentivized actor-critic (VAC) method for online RL, which jointly optimizes the QQ-function and the policy under function approximation over a single objective function. Different from MEX, VAC optimizes a regularized Lagrangian constructed with respect to the Bellman consistency equation as the constraint, naturally accommodating the interplay between the QQ-function and the policy. This formulation preserves the crux of optimistic regularization, while allowing differentiable optimization of the QQ-function and the policy simultaneously under general function approximation.

  • •

    Theoretical guarantees of VAC. We substantiate the efficacy of VAC with rigorous theoretical analysis, by proving it achieves a rate of O~​(d​H2​T)\widetilde{O}(dH^{2}\sqrt{T}) regret under the setting of episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) (Jin et al., 2020), where dd is the feature dimension, HH is the horizon length, and TT is the number of episodes. We further extend the analysis to the infinite-horizon discounted setting and the general function approximation setting under similar assumptions of prior art (Liu et al., 2024).

In sum, our work bridges the gap between theoretically efficient exploration principles and practical applicability in challenging online RL settings with function approximation.

1.2 Related work

We discuss a few lines of research that are closely related to our setting, focusing on those with theoretical guarantees under function approximation.

Regret bounds for online RL under function approximation.

Balancing the exploration-exploitation trade-off is of fundamental importance in the design of online RL algorithms. Most existing methods with provable guarantees rely on the construction of confidence sets and perform constrained optimization within the confident sets, including model-based (Wang et al., 2025; Foster et al., 2023b; Chen et al., 2025), value-based (Agarwal et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2023), policy optimization (Liu et al., 2023), and actor-critic (Tan et al., 2025) approaches, to name a few. Regret guarantees for approaches based on posterior sampling (Osband and Van Roy, 2017) are provided in (Zhong et al., 2022; Li and Luo, 2024; Agarwal and Zhang, 2022) under function approximation. Regret analysis under the linear MDP model (Jin et al., 2020) has also been actively established for various methods, e.g., for the episodic setting (Zanette et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2020; Papini et al., 2021) and for the infinite-horizon setting (Zhou et al., 2021; Moulin et al., 2025). However, the confident sets computation and posterior estimation are usually intractable with general function approximator, making the algorithm difficult to be applied.

Exploration via optimistic estimation.

Exploration via optimistic estimation has been actively studied recently due to its promise in practice, which has been examined over a wide range of settings such as bandits (Kumar and Becker, 1982; Liu et al., 2020; Hung et al., 2021), RL with human feedback (Cen et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), single-agent RL (Mete et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025), and Markov games (Foster et al., 2023a; Xiong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). Tailored to online RL, most of the optimistic estimation algorithms are model-based, with a few exceptions such as the model-free variant of MEX in (Liu et al., 2020), but still with computationally challenges.

Primal-dual optimization in RL.

Primal-dual formulation has been exploited in RL for handling the “double-sampling” issue (Dai et al., 2017; Dai et al., 2018) from an optimization perspective. By connecting through the linear programming view of MDP (De Farias and Van Roy, 2004; Puterman, 2014; Wang, 2017; Neu et al., 2017; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017; Bas-Serrano et al., 2021), a systematic framework (Nachum et al., 2019b) has been developed for offline RL, which induces concrete algorithms for off-policy evaluation (Nachum et al., 2019a; Uehara et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020), confidence interval evaluation (Dai et al., 2020), imitation learning (Kostrikov et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2022; Sikchi et al., 2023), and policy optimization (Nachum et al., 2019b; Lee et al., 2021). However, how to exploit the primal-dual formulation in online RL setting has not been investigated formally to the best of our knowledge.

Paper organization and notation.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We describe the background, and illuminate the connection between exploration and primal-dual optimization in Section 2. We present the proposed VAC method, and state its regret guarantee in Section 3. Finally, we conclude in Section 4. The proofs and generalizations to the infinite-horizon and general function approximation settings are deferred to the appendix.

2 Background and Motivation

2.1 Background

Episodic Markov decision processes.

Let ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,P,r,H)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,H) be a finite-horizon episodic MDP, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} denote the state space and the action space, respectively, H∈ℕ+H\in\mathbb{N}^{+} is the horizon length, and P={Ph}h∈[H]P=\{P_{h}\}_{h\in[H]} and r={rh}h∈[H]r=\{r_{h}\}_{h\in[H]} are the inhomogeneous transition kernel and the reward function: for each time step h∈[H]h\in[H], Ph:𝒮×𝒜↦Δ⁡(𝒮)P_{h}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mapsto\Delta(\mathcal{S}) specifies the probability distribution over the next state given the current state and action at step hh, and rh:𝒮×𝒜↦[0,1]r_{h}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mapsto[0,1] is the reward function at step hh. We let π={πh}h∈[H]:𝒮×[H]↦Δ⁡(A)\pi=\{\pi_{h}\}_{h\in[H]}:{\mathcal{S}}\times[H]\mapsto\Delta(A) denote the policy of the agent, where πh(⋅|s)∈Δ(𝒜)\pi_{h}(\cdot|s)\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}) specifies an action selection rule at time step hh.

For any given policy π\pi, the value function at step hh, denoted by Vhπ:𝒮↦ℝV^{\pi}_{h}:\mathcal{S}\mapsto\mathbb{R}, is given as

∀s∈𝒮,h∈[H]:Vhπ​(s)≔𝔼⁡[∑i=hHri​(si,ai)|sh=s],\textstyle\forall s\in\mathcal{S},\,h\in[H]:\quad V^{\pi}_{h}(s)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=h}^{H}r_{i}(s_{i},a_{i})|s_{h}=s\right], (1)

which measures the expected cumulative reward starting from state ss at time step hh until the end of the episode. The expectation is taken over the randomness of the trajectory generated following ai∼πi(⋅|si)a_{i}\sim\pi_{i}(\cdot|s_{i}) and the MDP dynamics si+1∼Pi(⋅|si,ai)s_{i+1}\sim P_{i}(\cdot|s_{i},a_{i}) for i=h,…,Hi=h,\dots,H. We define VHπ​(s)≔0V^{\pi}_{H}(s)\coloneqq 0 for all s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}. The value function at the beginning of the episode, when h=1h=1, is often denoted simply as Vπ​(s)≔V1π​(s)V^{\pi}(s)\coloneqq V^{\pi}_{1}(s). Given an initial state distribution s1∼ρs_{1}\sim\rho over 𝒮\mathcal{S}, we also define Vπ​(ρ)≔𝔼s1∼ρ​[V1π​(s1)]V^{\pi}(\rho)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{s_{1}\sim\rho}\left[V^{\pi}_{1}(s_{1})\right].

Similarly, the QQ-function of policy π\pi at step hh, denoted by Qhπ:𝒮×𝒜↦ℝQ^{\pi}_{h}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mapsto\mathbb{R}, is defined as

∀(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜,h∈[H]:Qhπ(s,a)≔𝔼[∑i=hHri(si,ai)|sh=s,ah=a],\textstyle\forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A},\,h\in[H]:\quad Q^{\pi}_{h}(s,a)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=h}^{H}r_{i}(s_{i},a_{i})|s_{h}=s,a_{h}=a\right], (2)

which measures the expected discounted cumulative reward starting from state ss and taking action aa at time step hh, and following policy π\pi thereafter, according to the time-dependent transitions. We define QH+1π​(s,a)≔0Q^{\pi}_{H+1}(s,a)\coloneqq 0 and Qπ​(s,a)≔Q1π​(s,a)Q^{\pi}(s,a)\coloneqq Q^{\pi}_{1}(s,a) for all (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}. They satisfy the Bellman consistency equation, given by, for all (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜,h∈[H](s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A},\,h\in[H]:

Qhπ(s,a)=rh(s,a)+𝔼sh+1∼Ph(⋅|s,a),ah+1∼πh+1(⋅|sh+1)[Qh+1π(sh+1,ah+1)].Q^{\pi}_{h}(s,a)=r_{h}(s,a)+\mathbb{E}_{s_{h+1}\sim P_{h}(\cdot|s,a),a_{h+1}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot|s_{h+1})}[Q^{\pi}_{h+1}(s_{h+1},a_{h+1})]. (3)

It is known that there exists at least one optimal policy π⋆=(π1⋆,…,πH⋆)\pi^{\star}=(\pi^{\star}_{1},\dots,\pi^{\star}_{H}) that maximizes the value function Vπ​(s)V^{\pi}(s) for all initial states s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} (Puterman, 2014). The corresponding optimal value function and Q-function are denoted as V⋆V^{\star} and Q⋆Q^{\star}, respectively. In particular, they satisfy the Bellman optimality equation, given by, for all (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜,h∈[H](s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A},\,h\in[H]:

Qh⋆(s,a)=rh(s,a)+𝔼sh+1∼Ph(⋅|s,a),ah+1∼πh+1⋆(⋅|sh+1)[Qh+1⋆(sh+1,ah+1)].Q^{\star}_{h}(s,a)=r_{h}(s,a)+\mathbb{E}_{s_{h+1}\sim P_{h}(\cdot|s,a),a_{h+1}\sim\pi_{h+1}^{\star}(\cdot|s_{h+1})}[Q^{\star}_{h+1}(s_{h+1},a_{h+1})]. (4)
Goal: regret minimization in online RL.

In this paper, we are interested in the online RL setting, where the agent interacts with the episodic MDP sequentially for TT episodes, where in the tt-th episode (t⩾1t\geqslant 1), the agent executes a policy πt={πt,h}h=1H\pi_{t}=\{\pi_{t,h}\}_{h=1}^{H} learned based on the data collected up to the (t−1)(t-1)-th episode. To evaluate the performance of the learned policy, our goal is to minimize the cumulative regret, defined as

𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝗍⁡(T)=∑t=1T(V⋆​(ρ)−Vπt​(ρ)),\displaystyle\textstyle\mathsf{Regret}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(V^{\star}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}(\rho)\right), (5)

which measures the sub-optimality gap between the values of the optimal policy and the learned policies over TT episodes. In particular, we would like the regret to scale sub-linearly in TT, so the sub-optimality gap is amortized over time.

2.2 Motivation: revisiting MEX from primal-dual lens

Recently, MEX (Liu et al., 2024) emerges as a promising framework for online RL, which balances exploration and exploitation in a single objective while naturally enabling function approximation. Consider a function class 𝒬=∏h=1H𝒬h\mathcal{Q}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{Q}_{h} of the QQ-function. For any f={fh}h∈[H]∈𝒬f=\{f_{h}\}_{h\in[H]}\in\mathcal{Q}, we denote the corresponding QQ-function Qf={Qf,h}h∈[H]Q_{f}=\{Q_{f,h}\}_{h\in[H]} with Qf,h=fhQ_{f,h}=f_{h}. At the beginning of the tt-th episode, given the collection 𝒟t−1,h\mathcal{D}_{t-1,h} of transition tuples (sh,sh,sh+1)(s_{h},s_{h},s_{h+1}) at step hh up to the (t−1)(t-1)-th episode, MEX (Liu et al., 2024) (more precisely, its model-free variant) updates the Q-function estimate as

ft=argsupf∈𝒬𝔼s1∼ρ[maxa∈𝒜Qf,1(s1,a)]−αℒt(f),\displaystyle f_{t}\;=\;\arg\sup_{f\in\mathcal{Q}}\;\mathbb{E}_{s_{1}\sim\rho}\Big[\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,1}(s_{1},a)\Big]\;-\;\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{t}(f), (6)

where α⩾0\alpha\geqslant 0 is some regularization parameter, and ℒt​(f)\mathcal{L}_{t}(f) is

ℒt(f)=∑h=1H\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}(f)=\sum_{h=1}^{H} [∑ξh∈𝒟t−1,h(rh(sh,ah)+maxa∈𝒜Qf,h+1(sh+1,a)−Qf,h(sh,ah))2\displaystyle\Bigg[\sum_{\xi_{h}\in\mathcal{D}_{t-1,h}}\big(r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,h+1}(s_{h+1},a)-Q_{f,h}(s_{h},a_{h})\big)^{2} (7)
−infgh∈𝒬h∑ξh∈𝒟t−1,h(rh(sh,ah)+maxa∈𝒜Qf,h+1(sh+1,a)−gh(sh,ah))2],\displaystyle\qquad-\inf_{g_{h}\in\mathcal{Q}_{h}}\sum_{\xi_{h}\in\mathcal{D}_{t-1,h}}\big(r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,h+1}(s_{h+1},a)-g_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\big)^{2}\Bigg],

where ξh=(sh,ah,sh+1)\xi_{h}=(s_{h},a_{h},s_{h+1}) is the transition tuple. The first term in (6) promotes exploration by searching for QQ-functions with higher values, while the second term ensures the Bellman consistency of the QQ-function with the collected data transitions. The policy is then updated greedily from QftQ_{f_{t}} to collect the next batch of data. While Liu et al. (2024) offered strong regret guarantees of MEX, there is little insight provided into the design of (6), which is deeply connected to the reward-biased framework in Kumar and Becker (1982).

Interpretation from primal-dual lens.

We offer a new interpretation of MEX, where optimistic regularization arises naturally from a regularized Lagrangian formulation of certain constrained value maximization problem within a primal-dual optimization perspective. As a brief detour to build intuition, we consider a value maximization problem over the Q-function with the exact (i.e., population) Bellman optimality equation as the constraints:

supf∈𝒬𝔼s1∼ρ​[maxa∈𝒜⁡Qf,1​(s1,a)]\displaystyle\sup_{f\in\mathcal{Q}}\;\,{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{1}\sim\rho}\Big[\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,1}(s_{1},a)\Big] (8)
s.t.Qf,h(s,a)=rh(s,a)+𝔼s′∼Ph(⋅∣s,a)[maxa∈𝒜Qf,h+1(s′,a)],∀(s,a,h)∈𝒮×𝒜×[H],\displaystyle\,\,\mathop{\mathrm{s.t.}}\,\,\,Q_{f,h}(s,a)=r_{h}(s,a)+{\mathbb{E}}_{s^{\prime}\sim P_{h}(\cdot\mid s,a)}\Big[\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a)\Big],\quad\forall(s,a,h)\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times[H],

with the boundary condition Qf,H+1=0Q_{f,H+1}=0. When the optimal QQ-function is realizable, i.e., Q⋆∈𝒬Q^{\star}\in\mathcal{Q}, the unique solution of (8) recovers the true optimal QQ-function Q⋆Q^{\star}.

How is this connected to the MEX objective? Introducing the dual variables {λh}h∈[H]\{\lambda_{h}\}_{h\in[H]}, the regularized Lagrangian of (8) can be written as

supf∈𝒬\displaystyle\sup_{f\in\mathcal{Q}}\; 𝔼s1∼ρ​[maxa∈𝒜⁡Qf,1​(s1,a)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s_{1}\sim\rho}\Big[\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,1}(s_{1},a)\Big]\; (9)
+inf{λh}h∈[H]∑h=1H𝔼(s,a,s′)∼𝒟h{λh(s,a)(rh(s,a)+maxa∈𝒜Qf,h+1(s′,a)−Qf,h(s,a))+β2λh(s,a)2},\displaystyle+\;\inf_{\{\lambda_{h}\}_{h\in[H]}}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}_{h}}\Big\{\lambda_{h}(s,a)\Big(r_{h}(s,a)+\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a)-Q_{f,h}(s,a)\Big)+\;\frac{\beta}{2}\,\lambda_{h}(s,a)^{2}\Big\},

where β>0\beta>0 is the regularization parameter of the dual variable,11 1 It is possible to use an (s,a,h)(s,a,h)-dependent regularization too. and 𝒟h\mathcal{D}_{h} denotes a properly defined joint distribution over the transition tuples that covers the state-action space over (s,a)(s,a). We invoke the trick in Dai et al. (2018); Baird (1995), which deals with the double-sampling issue, and reparameterize the dual variable

λh​(s,a)=Qf,h​(s,a)−gh​(s,a)β,\lambda_{h}(s,a)=\frac{Q_{f,h}(s,a)-g_{h}(s,a)}{\beta}, (10)

which satisfies

∀δh(s,a):λh(s,a)\displaystyle\forall\delta_{h}(s,a):\qquad\lambda_{h}(s,a) (δh​(s,a)−Qf,h​(s,a))+β2​λh​(s,a)2\displaystyle\big(\delta_{h}(s,a)-Q_{f,h}(s,a)\big)+\frac{\beta}{2}\lambda_{h}(s,a)^{2}
=12​β​[(δh​(s,a)−Qf,h​(s,a))2−(δh​(s,a)−gh​(s,a))2].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\beta}\Big[\big(\delta_{h}(s,a)-Q_{f,h}(s,a)\big)^{2}-\big(\delta_{h}(s,a)-g_{h}(s,a)\big)^{2}\Big]. (11)

Consequently, by setting δh​(s,a):=rh​(s,a)+maxa∈𝒜⁡Qf,h+1​(s′,a)\delta_{h}(s,a):=r_{h}(s,a)+\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a) in (11), the Lagrangian objective (9) becomes

supf∈𝒬𝔼s1∼ρ[maxa∈𝒜Qf,1(s1,a)]−∑h=1H12​βsupgh∈𝒬h𝔼(s,a,s′)∼𝒟h[(\displaystyle\sup_{f\in\mathcal{Q}}\;\mathbb{E}_{s_{1}\sim\rho}\Big[\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,1}(s_{1},a)\Big]-\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{1}{2\beta}\sup_{g_{h}\in\mathcal{Q}_{h}}\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}_{h}}\Big[\big( OPENrh​(s,a)+maxa∈𝒜⁡Qf,h+1​(s′,a)−Qf,h​(s,a))2\displaystyle r_{h}(s,a)+\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a)-Q_{f,h}(s,a)\big)^{2} (12)
−(rh(s,a)+maxa∈𝒜Qf,h+1(s′,a)−gh(s,a))2].\displaystyle-\big(r_{h}(s,a)+\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a)-g_{h}(s,a)\big)^{2}\Big].

By replacing the population distribution 𝒟h\mathcal{D}_{h} with its samples in 𝒟t−1,h\mathcal{D}_{t-1,h} at each round, then we recover the model-free MEX algorithm in (7).

However, (6) is a bilevel optimization problem where in the lower level, another optimization problem maxa∈𝒜⁡Qf,h​(s,a)\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{f,h}\left(s,a\right) needs to be computed in (7). This can be can be computationally intensive if not intractable. In this paper, inspired from this primal-dual view, we derive a more implementable algorithm.

3 Value-incentivized Actor-Critic Method

3.1 Algorithm development

We now develop the proposed value-incentivized actor-critic method. In contrast to the model-free MEX for (12), we consider a value maximization problem over both the QQ-function and the policy with the exact (i.e., population) Bellman consistency equation as the constraints:

supf∈𝒬,π∈𝒫\displaystyle\sup_{f\in\mathcal{Q},\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pi\in\mathcal{P}}}\; 𝔼s1∼ρ,a1∼π1(⋅∣s1)[Qf,1(s1,a1)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s_{1}\sim\rho,\;a_{1}\sim\pi_{1}(\cdot\mid s_{1})}\bigl[Q_{f,1}(s_{1},a_{1})\bigr] (13)
s.t. Qf,h​(s,a)=rh​(s,a)+𝔼s′∼Ph(⋅∣s,a)a′∼πh+1(⋅∣s′)​[Qf,h+1​(s′,a′)],∀(s,a,h)∈𝒮×𝒜×[H],\displaystyle Q_{f,h}(s,a)=r_{h}(s,a)+\mathbb{E}_{\,s^{\prime}\sim P_{h}(\cdot\mid s,a)\atop a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot\mid s^{\prime})}\bigl[Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\bigr],\qquad\forall\;(s,a,h)\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times[H],

where 𝒫=∏h=1H𝒫h\mathcal{P}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{P}_{h} is the policy class. This formulation explicits the joint optimization over the QQ-function (critic) and the policy (actor), and uses the Bellman’s consistency equation as the constraint, rather than the Bellman’s optimality equation, which is key to obtain a more tractable optimization problem.

Similar as (9), we can write the regularized Lagrangian of (13) as

supf∈𝒬,π∈𝒫𝔼s1∼ρ,a1∼π1(⋅∣s1)[Qf,1(s1,a1)]\displaystyle\sup_{f\in\mathcal{Q},\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pi\in\mathcal{P}}}\;\mathbb{E}_{s_{1}\sim\rho,\;a_{1}\sim\pi_{1}(\cdot\mid s_{1})}\bigl[Q_{f,1}(s_{1},a_{1})\bigr] (14)
+inf{λh}h=1H∑h=1H𝔼(s,a,s′)∼𝒟h𝔼a′∼πh+1(⋅|s′){λh(s,a)(rh(s,a)+Qf,h+1(s′,a′)−Qf,h(s,a))+β2λh(s,a)2}.\displaystyle+\inf_{\{\lambda_{h}\}_{h=1}^{H}}\;\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}_{h}}\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\Big\{\lambda_{h}(s,a)\Bigl(r_{h}(s,a)+Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-\,Q_{f,h}(s,a)\Bigr)+\frac{\beta}{2}\,\lambda_{h}(s,a)^{2}\Big\}.

Similar to earlier discussion, we also consider the reparameterization (10) which gives

supf,π∈𝒫{Vfπ(ρ)−∑h=1H12​βsupgh∈𝒬h𝔼(s,a,s′)∼𝒟h𝔼a′∼πh+1(⋅|s′)\displaystyle\sup_{f,{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\pi\in\mathcal{P}}}\;\Bigl\{\,V^{\pi}_{f}(\rho)-\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{1}{2\beta}\sup_{g_{h}\in\mathcal{Q}_{h}}\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}_{h}}\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot|s^{\prime})} [(rh(s,a)+Qf,h+1(s′,a′)−Qf,h(s,a))2\displaystyle\Bigl[\bigl(r_{h}(s,a)+Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-Q_{f,h}(s,a)\bigr)^{2}
−(rh(s,a)+Qf,h+1(s′,a′)−gh(s,a))2]},\displaystyle-\bigl(r_{h}(s,a)+Q_{f,h+1}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-g_{h}(s,a)\bigr)^{2}\Bigr]\Bigr\}, (15)

where we define

Vfπ(s)≔𝔼a∼π1(⋅|s)[Qf,1(s,a)],andVfπ(ρ)≔𝔼s∼ρ[Vfπ(s)].\displaystyle V^{\pi}_{f}(s)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{1}(\cdot|s)}\left[Q_{f,1}(s,a)\right],\quad\text{and}\quad V^{\pi}_{f}(\rho)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho}\left[V^{\pi}_{f}(s)\right]. (16)

Note that, the objective function (15) is easier to optimize over both QfQ_{f} and π\pi. Replacing the population distribution 𝒟h\mathcal{D}_{h} of ξ=(s,a,s′)\xi=(s,a,s^{\prime}) by its empirical samples leads to the proposed algorithm, which is termed value-incentivized actor-critic (VAC) method; see Algorithm 1 for a summary.

In Algorithm 1, at tt-th iteration, given dataset 𝒟t−1,h\mathcal{D}_{t-1,h} of transitions (sh,ah,sh+1)(s_{h},a_{h},s_{h+1}) collected from the previous iterations for all h∈[H]h\in[H], and use the current policy πt\pi_{t} to collect new action a′a^{\prime} for each tuples, we define the loss function as follows:

ℒt(f,π)=∑h=1H{\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}(f,\pi)=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\bigg\{ ∑ξh∈𝒟t−1,h𝔼a′∼πh+1(⋅∣sh+1)(rh(sh,ah)+Qf,h+1(sh+1,a′)−Qf,h(sh,ah))2\displaystyle\sum_{\xi_{h}\in\mathcal{D}_{t-1,h}}\mathbb{E}_{\,a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot\mid s_{h+1})}\bigl(r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+Q_{f,h+1}(s_{h+1},a^{\prime})-Q_{f,h}(s_{h},a_{h})\bigr)^{2}\quad
−infgh∈𝒬h∑ξh∈𝒟t−1,h𝔼a′∼πh+1(⋅∣sh+1)(rh(sh,ah)+Qf,h+1(sh+1,a′)−gh(sh,ah))2},\displaystyle-\inf_{g_{h}\in\mathcal{Q}_{h}}\sum_{\xi_{h}\in\mathcal{D}_{t-1,h}}\mathbb{E}_{\,a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot\mid s_{h+1})}\bigl(r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+Q_{f,h+1}(s_{h+1},a^{\prime})-g_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\bigr)^{2}\bigg\}, (18)

where ξh=(sh,ah,sh+1)\xi_{h}=(s_{h},a_{h},s_{h+1}) is the transition tuple. To approximately solve the optimization problem (17), which is the sample version of (15), we can, in practice, employ first-order method, i.e.,

  • •

    Critic evaluation: Given the policy πt−1\pi_{t-1} fixed, we solve the saddle-point problem for ftf_{t} as biased policy evaluation for πt−1\pi_{t-1}, i.e.,

    ft=arg⁡maxf∈𝒬​Vfπt−1​(ρ)−α​ℒt​(f,πt−1).f_{t}=\arg\max_{f\in\mathcal{Q}}\,\,V^{\pi_{t-1}}_{f}(\rho)-\alpha\mathcal{L}_{t}(f,\pi_{t-1}). (19)
  • •

    Policy update: Given the critic ff is fixed, we can update the policy π\pi through policy gradient following the gradient calculation in Nachum et al. (2019b).

Clearly, the proposed VAC recovers an actor-critic style algorithm, therefore, demonstrating the practical potential of the proposed algorithm. However, we emphasize the critic evaluation step is different from the vanilla policy evaluation, where we have Vfπ​(ρ)V^{\pi}_{f}(\rho) to bias the policy value. In contrast, MEX only admits an actor-critic implementation for α=0\alpha=0 (corresponding to vanilla actor-critic when there is no exploration) since their data loss term requires the optimal value function, while the data loss term ℒt​(f,π)\mathcal{L}_{t}(f,\pi) is policy-dependent in VAC.

3.2 Theoretical guarantees

The design of VAC is versatile and can be implemented with arbitrary function approximation. To corroborate its efficacy, however, we focus on understanding its theoretical performance in the linear MDP model, which is popular in the literature (Jin et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2021). Our analysis can be extended to general function approximation similar to the treatment in (Liu et al., 2024); see Appendix B.3 for more details.

Assumption 1 (linear MDP, Jin et al. (2020)).

There exist unknown vectors ζh∈ℝd\zeta_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and unknown (signed) measures μh=(μh(1),⋯,μh(d))\mu_{h}=(\mu_{h}^{(1)},\cdots,\mu_{h}^{(d)}) over 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} such that

rh​(s,a)=ϕh​(s,a)⊤​ζhandPh​(s′|s,a)=ϕh​(s,a)⊤​μh​(s′),\displaystyle r_{h}(s,a)=\phi_{h}(s,a)^{\top}\zeta_{h}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad P_{h}(s^{\prime}|s,a)=\phi_{h}(s,a)^{\top}\mu_{h}(s^{\prime}), (20)

where ϕh:𝒮×𝒜↦ℝd\phi_{h}:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{d} is a known feature map satisfying ‖ϕh​(s,a)‖2⩽1\|\phi_{h}(s,a)\|_{2}\leqslant 1, and max⁡{‖ζh‖2,‖μh​(𝒮)‖2}⩽d\max\{\left\|\zeta_{h}\right\|_{2},\left\|\mu_{h}({\mathcal{S}})\right\|_{2}\}\leqslant\sqrt{d}, for all (s,a,s′)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒮(s,a,s^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times{\mathcal{S}} and all h∈[H]h\in[H].

We also need to specify the function class 𝒬\mathcal{Q} for the QQ-function and the policy class 𝒫\mathcal{P} for the policy. Under the linear MDP, it suffices to represent QQ-function linearly w.r.t. ϕh​(s,a)\phi_{h}\left(s,a\right), i.e., Qh​(s,a)=ϕh​(s,a)⊤​θhQ_{h}\left(s,a\right)=\phi_{h}\left(s,a\right)^{\top}\theta_{h}, and the log-linear function approximation for the policy derived from the max-entropy policy (Ren et al., 2022), with the following two regularization assumptions on the weights.

Assumption 2 (linear QQ-function class).

The function class 𝒬=∏h=1H𝒬h\mathcal{Q}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{Q}_{h} is

∀h∈[H]:𝒬h≔{fθ,h≔ϕh(⋅,⋅)⊤θ:‖θ‖2⩽(H+1−h)d,‖fθ,h‖∞⩽H+1−h}.\forall h\in[H]:\;\mathcal{Q}_{h}\coloneqq\left\{f_{\theta,h}\coloneqq\phi_{h}(\cdot,\cdot)^{\top}\theta:\left\|\theta\right\|_{2}\leqslant(H+1-h)\sqrt{d},\,\left\|f_{\theta,h}\right\|_{\infty}\leqslant H+1-h\right\}.
Assumption 3 (log-linear policy class).

The policy class 𝒫=∏h=1H𝒫h\mathcal{P}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{P}_{h} is

∀h∈[H]:𝒫h≔{πω,h:πω,h​(a|s)=exp⁡(ϕh​(s,a)⊤​ω)∑a′∈𝒜exp⁡(ϕh​(s,a′)⊤​ω)​with​‖ω‖2⩽B​H​d}\forall h\in[H]:\quad\mathcal{P}_{h}\coloneqq\left\{\pi_{\omega,h}:\pi_{\omega,h}(a|s)=\frac{\exp\left(\phi_{h}(s,a)^{\top}\omega\right)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\exp\left(\phi_{h}(s,a^{\prime})^{\top}\omega\right)}\,\,\text{with}\,\,\left\|\omega\right\|_{2}\leqslant BH\sqrt{d}\right\}

with some constant B>0B>0.

Under these assumptions, we first state the regret bound of Algorithm 1 in Theorem 1.

Theorem 1.

Suppose Assumptions 1-3 hold. We let B=T​log⁡|𝒜|d​HB=\frac{T\log|\mathcal{A}|}{dH} in Assumption 3, and set

α=(1H2​T​log⁡(log⁡|𝒜|​T/δ)​log⁡(1+T3/2d))1/2.\displaystyle\alpha=\left(\frac{1}{H^{2}T\log\left(\log|\mathcal{A}|T/\delta\right)}\log\left(1+\frac{T^{3/2}}{d}\right)\right)^{1/2}. (21)

Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the regret of VAC (cf. Algorithm 1) satisfies

𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝗍⁡(T)=𝒪⁡(d​H2​T​log⁡(log⁡(|𝒜|)​Tδ)​log⁡(1+T3/2d)).\displaystyle\mathsf{Regret}(T)=\mathcal{O}\left(dH^{2}\sqrt{T}\sqrt{\log\left(\frac{\log(|\mathcal{A}|)T}{\delta}\right)\log\left(1+\frac{T^{3/2}}{d}\right)}\right). (22)

Theorem 1 shows that by choosing B=O~​(T/d​H)B=\widetilde{O}(T/dH) and α=O~​(1H​T)\alpha=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{H\sqrt{T}}\right), the regret of VAC is no larger than the order of O~​(d​H2​T)\widetilde{O}(dH^{2}\sqrt{T}) up to log\log-factors. Compared to the minimax lower bound Ω~​(d​H3​T)\widetilde{\Omega}(d\sqrt{H^{3}T}) (He et al., 2023), this suggests that our bound is near-optimal up to a factor of H\sqrt{H}, but with practical implementation generalizable to arbitrary function approximator.

Extension to the infinite-horizon setting.

Our algorithm and theory can be extended to the infinite-horizon discounted setting leveraging the sampling procedure in Yuan et al. (2023, Algorithm 3). We demonstrate that the sample complexity of VAC is no larger than O~​(d2(1−γ)5​ε2)\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{d^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{5}\varepsilon^{2}}\right) to return an ε\varepsilon-optimal policy, where γ\gamma is the discount factor. This rate is near-optimal up to polynomial factors of 11−γ\frac{1}{1-\gamma} and logarithmic factors. We leave the details to the appendix.

4 Conclusion

In this paper, we develop a provably sample-efficient actor-critic method, called value-incentivized actor-critic (VAC), for online RL with a single easy-to-optimize objective function that avoids complex bilevel optimization in the presence of complex function approximation. We theoretically establish VAC’s efficacy by proving it achieves O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})-regret in both episodic and discounted settings. Our work suggests that a unified Lagrangian-based objective offers a promising direction for principled and practical online RL, allowing many venues for future developments. Follow-up efforts will focus on empirical validation, and extending the algorithm design to multi-agent settings.

Appendix A Technical Lemmas

We provide some technical lemmas that will be used in our proofs.

Lemma 1 (Freedman’s inequality, Lemma D.2 in Liu et al. [2024]).

Let {Xt}t⩽T\{X_{t}\}_{t\leqslant T} be a real-valued martingale difference sequence adapted to filtration {ℱt}t⩽T\{\mathcal{F}_{t}\}_{t\leqslant T}. If |Xt|⩽R|X_{t}|\leqslant R almost surely, then for any η∈(0,1/R)\eta\in(0,1/R) it holds that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

∑t=1TXt⩽𝒪⁡(η​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[Xt2|ℱt−1]+log⁡(1/δ)η).\sum_{t=1}^{T}X_{t}\leqslant\mathcal{O}\left(\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[X_{t}^{2}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\eta}\right).
Lemma 2 (Covering number of ℓ2\ell_{2} ball, Lemma D.5 in Jin et al. [2020]).

For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and d∈ℕ+d\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, the ϵ\epsilon-covering number of the ℓ2\ell_{2} ball of radius RR in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is bounded by (1+2​R/ϵ)d(1+2R/\epsilon)^{d}.

Lemma 3 (Lemma 11 in Abbasi-Yadkori et al. [2011]).

Let {xs}s∈[T]\{x_{s}\}_{s\in[T]} be a sequence of vectors with xs∈𝒱x_{s}\in\mathcal{V} for some Hilbert space 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Let Λ0\Lambda_{0} be a positive definite matrix and define Λt=Λ0+∑s=1txs​xs⊤\Lambda_{t}=\Lambda_{0}+\sum_{s=1}^{t}x_{s}x_{s}^{\top}. Then it holds that

∑s=1Tmin⁡{1,‖xs‖Λs−1−1}⩽2​log⁡(det(ΛT)det(Λ0)).\displaystyle\sum_{s=1}^{T}\min\left\{1,\|x_{s}\|_{\Lambda_{s-1}^{-1}}\right\}\leqslant 2\log\left(\frac{\det(\Lambda_{T})}{\det(\Lambda_{0})}\right).
Lemma 4 (Lemma F.3 in Du et al. [2021]).

Let 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and supx∈𝒳‖x‖2⩽BX\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\left\|x\right\|_{2}\leqslant B_{X}. Then for any n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, we have

∀λ>0:maxx1,⋯,xn∈𝒳​log​det(Id+1λ​∑i=1nxi​xi⊤)⩽d​log⁡(1+n​BX2d​λ).\displaystyle\forall\lambda>0:\quad\max_{x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}\in\mathcal{X}}\log\det\left(I_{d}+\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)\leqslant d\log\left(1+\frac{nB_{X}^{2}}{d\lambda}\right).
Lemma 5 (Corollary A.7 in Edelman et al. [2022]).

Define the softmax function as 𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑⁡(⋅):ℝd→Δd\mathsf{softmax}(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\Delta^{d} by 𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑​(x)i=exp⁡(xi)∑j=1dexp⁡(xj)\mathsf{softmax}(x)_{i}=\frac{\exp(x_{i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}\exp(x_{j})} for all i∈[d]i\in[d] and x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then for any x,y∈ℝdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have

‖𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑⁡(x)−𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑⁡(y)‖1⩽2​‖x−y‖∞.\displaystyle\|\mathsf{softmax}(x)-\mathsf{softmax}(y)\|_{1}\leqslant 2\|x-y\|_{\infty}.

B.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Notation and preparation.

For notation simplicity, we let f⋆≔Q⋆f^{\star}\coloneqq Q^{\star} be the optimal Q-function. We let Π≔Δ​(𝒜)𝒮\Pi\coloneqq\Delta(\mathcal{A})^{\mathcal{S}} denote the whole policy space. We have 𝒫h⊂Π\mathcal{P}_{h}\subset\Pi for all h∈[H]h\in[H]. We also define the transition tuples

ξ≔(s,a,s′)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒮andξh≔(sh,ah,sh+1)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒮.\displaystyle\xi\coloneqq(s,a,s^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times{\mathcal{S}}\quad\text{and}\quad\xi_{h}\coloneqq(s_{h},a_{h},s_{h+1})\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times{\mathcal{S}}. (23)

Given any policy profile π={πh}h∈[H]\pi=\{\pi_{h}\}_{h\in[H]} and f={fh:𝒮×𝒜↦ℝ}f=\left\{f_{h}:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\mapsto\mathbb{R}\right\}, we define ℙhπ​f\mathbb{P}_{h}^{\pi}f as

∀(sh,ah)∈𝒮×𝒜:ℙhπ​f​(sh,ah)≔rh​(sh,ah)+𝔼sh+1∼ℙh(⋅|sh,ah),ah+1∼πh+1(⋅|sh+1)​[fh+1​(sh+1,ah+1)],\displaystyle\forall(s_{h},a_{h})\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}:\quad\mathbb{P}_{h}^{\pi}f(s_{h},a_{h})\coloneqq r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+\mathbb{E}_{s_{h+1}\sim\mathbb{P}_{h}(\cdot|s_{h},a_{h}),\atop a_{h+1}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot|s_{h+1})}\left[f_{h+1}(s_{h+1},a_{h+1})\right], (24)

and let ℙπ​f≔{ℙhπ​f}h∈[H]\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f\coloneqq\{\mathbb{P}_{h}^{\pi}f\}_{h\in[H]}. Let

Θh≔{θ:fθ,h∈𝒬h},Ω≔{ω:‖ω‖2⩽B​H​d}\displaystyle\Theta_{h}\coloneqq\{\theta:f_{\theta,h}\in\mathcal{Q}_{h}\},\quad\Omega\coloneqq\left\{\omega:\left\|\omega\right\|_{2}\leqslant BH\sqrt{d}\right\} (25)

be the parameter space of 𝒬h\mathcal{Q}_{h} and 𝒫h\mathcal{P}_{h}, respectively for all h∈[H]h\in[H]. We also define

Vf,hπ(s)≔𝔼a∼π(⋅|s)[Qf,h(s,a)]andVf,hπ(ρ)≔𝔼s∼ρ[Vf,hπ(s)],∀f∈𝒬,π∈𝒫,s∈𝒮,h∈[H].\displaystyle V_{f,h}^{\pi}(s)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}\left[Q_{f,h}(s,a)\right]\quad\text{and}\quad V_{f,h}^{\pi}(\rho)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho}\left[V_{f,h}^{\pi}(s)\right],\quad\forall f\in\mathcal{Q},\pi\in\mathcal{P},s\in{\mathcal{S}},h\in[H]. (26)

We’ll repeatedly use the following lemma, which guarantees that under Assumption 1, the optimal Q-function Q⋆Q^{\star} is in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and ℙπ​f∈𝒬\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f\in\mathcal{Q} for any f∈𝒬f\in\mathcal{Q} and π∈ΠH\pi\in\Pi^{H}. Similar results can be found in the literature, e.g., Jin et al. [2020]. For completeness, we include the proof of Lemma 6 in Appendix B.2.1.

Lemma 6 (Linear MDP ⇒\Rightarrow Bellman completeness + realizability).

Under Assumption 1, we have

  • •

    (realizability) Q⋆∈𝒬Q^{\star}\in\mathcal{Q};

  • •

    (Bellman completeness) ∀π∈Π\forall\pi\in\Pi and f∈𝒬f\in\mathcal{Q}, ℙπ​f∈𝒬\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f\in\mathcal{Q}.

We also use the following lemma, which bounds the difference between the optimal value function V⋆V^{\star} and maxπ∈𝒫⁡Vπ\max_{\pi\in\mathcal{P}}V^{\pi} — the optimal value over the policy class 𝒫\mathcal{P}, where we let

π~h⋆≔arg⁡maxπh∈𝒫h​Vf⋆,hπ​(ρ),∀h∈[H],\displaystyle\widetilde{\pi}_{h}^{\star}\coloneqq\arg\max_{\pi_{h}\in\mathcal{P}_{h}}V_{f^{\star},h}^{\pi}(\rho),\quad\forall h\in[H], (27)

and π~⋆={π~h⋆}h∈[H]\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}=\{\widetilde{\pi}_{h}^{\star}\}_{h\in[H]} be the optimal policy within the policy class 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The proof of Lemma 7 is deferred to Appendix B.2.2.

Lemma 7 (model error with log-linear policies).

Under Assumptions 1-3, we have

∀s∈𝒮,h∈[H]:0⩽Vh⋆​(s)−Vf⋆,hπ~⋆​(s)⩽log⁡|𝒜|B,\displaystyle\forall s\in{\mathcal{S}},h\in[H]:\quad 0\leqslant V^{\star}_{h}(s)-V_{f^{\star},h}^{\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}}(s)\leqslant\frac{\log|\mathcal{A}|}{B}, (28)

where BB is defined in Assumption 3.

Main proof.

We first decompose the regret (cf. (5)) as follows:

𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝗍⁡(T)=∑t=1T(V⋆​(ρ)−Vπt​(ρ))=∑t=1T(V⋆​(ρ)−Vftπt​(ρ))⏟(i)+∑t=1T(Vftπt​(ρ)−Vπt​(ρ))⏟(ii),\displaystyle\mathsf{Regret}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(V^{\star}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}(\rho)\right)=\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(V^{\star}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}_{f_{t}}(\rho)\right)}_{\text{(i)}}+\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(V^{\pi_{t}}_{f_{t}}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}(\rho)\right)}_{\text{(ii)}}, (29)

where recall we define Vfπ=Vf,1πV^{\pi}_{f}=V^{\pi}_{f,1} in (16). We will bound the two terms separately.

Step 1: bounding term (i).

The linear MDP assumption guarantees that Q⋆∈𝒬Q^{\star}\in\mathcal{Q} by Lemma 6, and by definition (27), π~⋆\widetilde{\pi}^{\star} is in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Thus by our update rule (17), we have

∀t∈ℕ+:Vf⋆π~⋆​(ρ)−α​ℒt​(f⋆,π~⋆)⩽Vftπt​(ρ)−α​ℒt​(ft,πt),\displaystyle\forall t\in\mathbb{N}_{+}:\quad V_{f^{\star}}^{\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}}(\rho)-\alpha\mathcal{L}_{t}(f^{\star},{\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}})\leqslant V^{\pi_{t}}_{f_{t}}(\rho)-\alpha\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{t},\pi_{t}),

which gives

Vf⋆π~⋆​(ρ)−Vftπt​(ρ)\displaystyle V_{f^{\star}}^{\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}_{f_{t}}(\rho) ⩽α⁡(ℒt​(f⋆,π~⋆)−ℒt​(ft,πt)).\displaystyle\leqslant\alpha\left(\mathcal{L}_{t}(f^{\star},\widetilde{\pi}^{\star})-\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{t},\pi_{t})\right).

Invoking Lemma 7, we have

V⋆​(ρ)−Vftπt​(ρ)\displaystyle V^{\star}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}_{f_{t}}(\rho) ⩽α⁡(ℒt​(f⋆,π~⋆)−ℒt​(ft,πt))+log⁡|𝒜|B.\displaystyle\leqslant\alpha\left(\mathcal{L}_{t}(f^{\star},\widetilde{\pi}^{\star})-\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{t},\pi_{t})\right)+\frac{\log|\mathcal{A}|}{B}. (30)

Thus to bound (i), it suffices to bound ℒt​(f⋆,π~⋆)−ℒt​(ft,πt)\mathcal{L}_{t}(f^{\star},\widetilde{\pi}^{\star})-\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{t},\pi_{t}) for each t∈[T]t\in[T]. To introduce our lemmas, we define ℓh:𝒬h×𝒮×𝒜×Π↦ℝ\ell_{h}:\mathcal{Q}_{h}\times{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times\Pi\mapsto\mathbb{R} for all h∈[H]h\in[H] as

ℓh​(f,s,a,π)≔(𝔼s′∼ℙh(⋅|s,a),a′∼πh+1(⋅|s′)​[rh​(s,a)+fh+1​(s′,a′)−fh​(s,a)])2.\displaystyle\ell_{h}(f,s,a,\pi)\coloneqq\left(\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim\mathbb{P}_{h}(\cdot|s,a),\atop a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\left[r_{h}(s,a)+f_{h+1}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-f_{h}(s,a)\right]\right)^{2}. (31)

We give the following lemma that bounds (i), whose proof is given in Appendix B.2.3.

Lemma 9.

Under Assumption 1, for any η>0\eta>0, we have

∑t=1T|Vftπt​(ρ)−Vπt​(ρ)|\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|V_{f_{t}}^{\pi_{t}}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}(\rho)\right| ⩽η​∑t=1T∑i=1t−1∑h=1H𝔼(si,ai)∼dρ,hπi​ℓh​(ft,si,ai,πt)+(6​H2+H/η)​d​(λ)+H2​λ​d​T.\displaystyle\leqslant\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{(s_{i},a_{i})\sim d^{\pi_{i}}_{\rho,h}}\ell_{h}(f_{t},s_{i},a_{i},\pi_{t})+(6H^{2}+H/\eta)d(\lambda)+H^{2}\lambda dT.

By Lemma 9, we have

(ii) ⩽η​∑t=1T∑i=1t−1∑h=1H𝔼(si,ai)∼dρ,hπi​ℓh​(ft,si,ai,πt)+(6​H2+H/η)​d​(λ)+H2​λ​d​T.\displaystyle\leqslant\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{(s_{i},a_{i})\sim d^{\pi_{i}}_{\rho,h}}\ell_{h}(f_{t},s_{i},a_{i},\pi_{t})+(6H^{2}+H/\eta)d(\lambda)+H^{2}\lambda dT. (35)

+(6​H2+2​H/α)​d​(λ)+H2​λ​d​T.\displaystyle+(6H^{2}+2H/\alpha)d(\lambda)+H^{2}\lambda dT. (36)

Assumption 1 guarantees that

Qh⋆​(sh,ah)\displaystyle Q_{h}^{\star}(s_{h},a_{h}) =rh(sh,ah)+𝔼sh+1∼ℙh(⋅|sh,ah)[Vh+1⋆(sh+1)]\displaystyle=r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+\mathbb{E}_{s_{h+1}\sim\mathbb{P}_{h}(\cdot|s_{h},a_{h})}\left[V^{\star}_{h+1}(s_{h+1})\right]

=ϕh​(sh,ah)⊤​(ζh+∫𝒮Vh+1⋆​(sh+1)​d​μh​(sh+1)⏟≔νh⋆),\displaystyle=\phi_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})^{\top}\Big(\underbrace{\zeta_{h}+\int_{{\mathcal{S}}}V^{\star}_{h+1}(s_{h+1})d\mu_{h}(s_{h+1})}_{\coloneqq\nu_{h}^{\star}}\Big), (37)

⩽‖ζh‖2+‖Vh+1⋆‖∞​‖μh​(𝒮)‖2⩽d+(H−h)​d=d​(H−h+1).\displaystyle\leqslant\left\|\zeta_{h}\right\|_{2}+\left\|V^{\star}_{h+1}\right\|_{\infty}\left\|\mu_{h}({\mathcal{S}})\right\|_{2}\leqslant\sqrt{d}+(H-h)\sqrt{d}=\sqrt{d}(H-h+1).

=ϕh​(sh,ah)⊤​(ζh+∫𝒮(𝔼ah+1∼πh+1(⋅|sh+1)fh+1(sh+1,ah+1))dμh(sh+1)⏟≔ζh),\displaystyle=\phi_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})^{\top}\Big(\underbrace{\zeta_{h}+\int_{{\mathcal{S}}}\left(\mathbb{E}_{a_{h+1}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot|s_{h+1})}f_{h+1}(s_{h+1},a_{h+1})\right)d\mu_{h}(s_{h+1})}_{\coloneqq\zeta_{h}}\Big),

B.2.2 Proof of Lemma 7

From Lemma 6, it is known that for all h∈[H]h\in[H], there exists νh⋆∈Θh\nu_{h}^{\star}\in\Theta_{h} such that

0⩽ℋ⁡(p)⩽log⁡|𝒜|,∀p∈Δ⁡(𝒜).\displaystyle 0\leqslant\mathcal{H}(p)\leqslant\log|\mathcal{A}|,\quad\forall p\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}). (41)

We bound the two terms ℒt​(f⋆,π~⋆)\mathcal{L}_{t}(f^{\star},\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}) and −ℒt​(ft,πt)-\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{t},\pi_{t}) on the left-hand side of (32) separately.

−infg∈𝒬∑i=1t−1𝔼a′∼πh+1(⋅|si,h+1)[(rh(si,h,ai,h)+fh+1(si,h+1,a′)−g(si,h,ai,h))2].\displaystyle\quad-\inf_{g\in\mathcal{Q}}\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{h+1}(\cdot|s_{i,h+1})}\left[\bigl(r_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})+f_{h+1}(s_{i,h+1},a^{\prime})-g(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})\bigr)^{2}\right]. (49)

Therefore, to upper bound −ℒt(ft,πt)=−∑h=1Hℒt,h(ft,πt)-\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{t},\pi_{t})=-\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{L}_{t,h}(f_{t},\pi_{t}), it suffices to bound −∑i=1t−1Xft,πt,hi-\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}X_{f_{t},\pi_{t},h}^{i} for all h∈[H]h\in[H]. In what follows, we use Freedman’s inequality (Lemma 1) and a covering number argument similar to that in Yang et al. [2025] to give the desired bound.

Step 1.1: building the covering argument.

We start with some basic preparation on the covering argument. For any 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, let 𝒩⁡(𝒳,ϵ,‖⋅‖)\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X},\epsilon,\left\|\cdot\right\|) be the ϵ\epsilon-covering number of 𝒳\mathcal{X} with respect to the norm ‖⋅‖\left\|\cdot\right\|. Assumption 2 and Assumption 3 guarantee that (cf. (25)) Θh⊂𝔹2d​(H​d)\Theta_{h}\subset\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}\left(H\sqrt{d}\right) and Ω=𝔹2d​(B​H​d)\Omega=\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}\left(BH\sqrt{d}\right) for all hh, where we use 𝔹2d​(R)\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}(R) to denote the ℓ2\ell_{2} ball of radius RR in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Thus by Lemma 2 we have

log⁡𝒩⁡(Θh,ϵ,‖⋅‖2)\displaystyle\log\mathcal{N}\left(\Theta_{h},\epsilon,\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}\right) ⩽log⁡𝒩⁡(𝔹2d​(H​d),ϵ,‖⋅‖2)⩽d​log⁡(1+2​H​dϵ),\displaystyle\leqslant\log\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}\left(H\sqrt{d}\right),\epsilon,\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}\right)\leqslant d\log\left(1+\frac{2H\sqrt{d}}{\epsilon}\right), (50a)
log⁡𝒩⁡(Ω,ϵ,‖⋅‖2)\displaystyle\log\mathcal{N}(\Omega,\epsilon,\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}) =log⁡𝒩⁡(𝔹2d​(B​H​d),ϵ,‖⋅‖2)⩽d​log⁡(1+2​B​H​dϵ)\displaystyle=\log\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}\left(BH\sqrt{d}\right),\epsilon,\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}\right)\leqslant d\log\left(1+\frac{2BH\sqrt{d}}{\epsilon}\right) (50b)

for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0. This suggests that for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists an ϵ\epsilon-net Θh,ϵ⊂Θh\Theta_{h,\epsilon}\subset\Theta_{h} and an ϵ\epsilon-net Ωϵ⊂Ω\Omega_{\epsilon}\subset\Omega such that

log|Θh,ϵ|⩽d​log⁡(1+2​H​dϵ),andlog|Ωϵ|⩽d​log⁡(1+2​B​H​dϵ).\displaystyle\log|\Theta_{h,\epsilon}|\leqslant d\log\left(1+\frac{2H\sqrt{d}}{\epsilon}\right),\quad\text{and}\quad\log|\Omega_{\epsilon}|\leqslant d\log\left(1+\frac{2BH\sqrt{d}}{\epsilon}\right). (51)

For any fh=fθ,h∈𝒬hf_{h}=f_{\theta,h}\in\mathcal{Q}_{h} with θh∈Θh\theta_{h}\in\Theta_{h}, there exists θh,ϵ∈Θh,ϵ\theta_{h,\epsilon}\in\Theta_{h,\epsilon} such that ‖θh−θh,ϵ‖2⩽ϵ\|\theta_{h}-\theta_{h,\epsilon}\|_{2}\leqslant\epsilon, and we let fh,ϵ≔fθh,ϵf_{h,\epsilon}\coloneqq f_{\theta_{h,\epsilon}} and define

𝒬h,ϵ≔{fh,ϵ:θh,ϵ∈Θh,ϵ},𝒬ϵ=∏h=1H𝒬h,ϵ\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{h,\epsilon}\coloneqq\{f_{h,\epsilon}:\theta_{h,\epsilon}\in\Theta_{h,\epsilon}\},\qquad\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{Q}_{h,\epsilon} (52)

In addition, for any πh∈𝒫h\pi_{h}\in\mathcal{P}_{h}, there exists ωh∈Ω\omega_{h}\in\Omega and ωh,ϵ∈Ωϵ\omega_{h,\epsilon}\in\Omega_{\epsilon} such that ‖ωh−ωh,ϵ‖2⩽ϵ\|\omega_{h}-\omega_{h,\epsilon}\|_{2}\leqslant\epsilon, such that

πh​(a|s)=exp⁡(ϕh​(s,a)⊤​ωh)∑a′∈𝒜exp⁡(ϕh​(s,a′)⊤​ωh),πh,ϵ​(a|s)≔exp⁡(ϕh​(s,a)⊤​ωh,ϵ)∑a′∈𝒜exp⁡(ϕh​(s,a′)⊤​ωh,ϵ),∀(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜.\pi_{h}(a|s)=\frac{\exp(\phi_{h}(s,a)^{\top}\omega_{h})}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\exp(\phi_{h}(s,a^{\prime})^{\top}\omega_{h})},\qquad\pi_{h,\epsilon}(a|s)\coloneqq\frac{\exp(\phi_{h}(s,a)^{\top}\omega_{h,\epsilon})}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\exp(\phi_{h}(s,a^{\prime})^{\top}\omega_{h,\epsilon})},\quad\forall(s,a)\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}.

We define

𝒫h,ϵ≔{πh,ϵ:ωh,ϵ∈Ωϵ},𝒫ϵ=∏h=1H𝒫h,ϵ.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{h,\epsilon}\coloneqq\{\pi_{h,\epsilon}:\omega_{h,\epsilon}\in\Omega_{\epsilon}\},\qquad\mathcal{P}_{\epsilon}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{P}_{h,\epsilon}. (53)

We claim that for any f∈𝒬f\in\mathcal{Q} and π∈𝒫\pi\in\mathcal{P}, there exists fϵ∈𝒬ϵf_{\epsilon}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon} and πϵ∈𝒫ϵ\pi_{\epsilon}\in\mathcal{P}_{\epsilon} such that

|Xfϵ,πϵ,ht−Xf,π,ht|\displaystyle\left|X_{f_{\epsilon},\pi_{\epsilon},h}^{t}-X_{f,\pi,h}^{t}\right| ⩽24​H2​ϵ.\displaystyle\leqslant 24H^{2}\epsilon. (54)

The proof of (54) is deferred to the end of this proof.

B.3 Extension to general function approximation

We now extend the analysis to finite-horizon MDPs with general function approximation. We first state our assumptions in this section.

Assumption 4 (Q-function class).

The Q-function class 𝒬=∏h=1H𝒬h\mathcal{Q}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{Q}_{h} satisfies

  • •

    (realizability) Q⋆∈𝒬Q^{\star}\in\mathcal{Q}.

  • •

    (Bellman completeness) ∀π∈𝒫\forall\pi\in\mathcal{P} and f∈𝒬f\in\mathcal{Q}, ℙπ​f∈𝒬\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f\in\mathcal{Q}.

  • •

    (boundedness) ∀fh∈𝒬h\forall f_{h}\in\mathcal{Q}_{h}, ‖fh‖∞⩽H+1−h\left\|f_{h}\right\|_{\infty}\leqslant H+1-h.

Assumption 4 is a standard condition in prior literature involving general function approximation [Liu et al., 2024, Assumption 3.1], [Jin et al., 2021, Assumption 2.1]. In particular, Assumption 4 holds under linear MDPs (c.f. Assumption 1), as established inLemma 6. Under Assumption 4, we set the policy class 𝒫\mathcal{P} as follows.

Assumption 5 (Policy class).

The policy class 𝒫=∏h=1H𝒫h\mathcal{P}=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{P}_{h} is

∀h∈[H]:𝒫h≔{πh:πh(s,a)=exp⁡(B​Qh​(s,a))∑a′∈𝒜exp⁡(B​Qh​(s,a′)),∀Qh∈𝒬h}\displaystyle\forall h\in[H]:\quad\mathcal{P}_{h}\coloneqq\left\{\pi_{h}:\pi_{h}(s,a)=\frac{\exp\left(BQ_{h}(s,a)\right)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\exp\left(BQ_{h}(s,a^{\prime})\right)},\,\,\forall Q_{h}\in\mathcal{Q}_{h}\right\} (114)

with some constant B>0B>0.

Moreover, drawing upon the work of Zhong et al. [2022], Liu et al. [2024], we require the MDP to feature a low generalized Eluder coefficient (GEC). This characteristic is essential for ensuring that the minimization of in-sample prediction error, based on historical data, also effectively limits out-of-sample prediction error.

Assumption 6 (Generalized Eluder coefficient, Assumption 4.2 in Liu et al. [2024]).

Given any λ~>0\widetilde{\lambda}>0, there exists d~​(λ~)∈ℝ+\widetilde{d}(\widetilde{\lambda})\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that for any sequence {ft}t=1T⊂𝒬\{f_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\subset\mathcal{Q}, {πt}t=1T⊂𝒫\{\pi_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\subset\mathcal{P}, we have

∑t=1T(Vftπt​(ρ)−Vπt​(ρ))⩽infη>0η​∑t=1T∑i=1t−1∑h=1H𝔼(si,ai)∼dρ,hπi​ℓh​(ft,si,ai,πt)+d~​(λ~)η+d~​(λ~)​H​T+λ~​H​T.\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(V_{f_{t}}^{\pi_{t}}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}(\rho)\right)\leqslant\inf_{\eta>0}\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{(s_{i},a_{i})\sim d^{\pi_{i}}_{\rho,h}}\ell_{h}(f_{t},s_{i},a_{i},\pi_{t})+\frac{\widetilde{d}(\widetilde{\lambda})}{\eta}+\sqrt{\widetilde{d}(\widetilde{\lambda})HT}+\widetilde{\lambda}HT. (115)

For each λ~>0\widetilde{\lambda}>0, we denote the smallest d~​(λ~)∈ℝ+\widetilde{d}(\widetilde{\lambda})\in\mathbb{R}_{+} that makes (115) hold as dGEC​(λ~)d_{\textsf{GEC}}(\widetilde{\lambda}).

From Lemma 9 we can see that under linear MDPs (c.f. Assumption 1), Assumption 6 holds with dGEC​(λ~)≲H​d​(λ~d​H)d_{\textsf{GEC}}(\widetilde{\lambda})\lesssim Hd\left(\frac{\widetilde{\lambda}}{dH}\right), where d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) is defined in (34). Moreover, as demonstrated by Zhong et al. [2022], RL problems characterized by a low Generalized Eluder Coefficient (GEC) constitute a significantly broad category, such as linear MDPs [Yang and Wang, 2019, Jin et al., 2020], linear mixture MDPs [Ayoub et al., 2020], MDPs of bilinear classes [Du et al., 2021], MDPs with low witness rank [Sun et al., 2019], and MDPs with low Bellman Eluder dimension [Jin et al., 2021], see Zhong et al. [2022] for a more detailed discussion.

We let 𝒩⁡(𝒬h,ϵ,‖⋅‖∞)\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{Q}_{h},\epsilon,\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\infty}) denote the ϵ\epsilon-covering number of 𝒬h\mathcal{Q}_{h} w.r.t. the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm, and assume the ϵ\epsilon-nets 𝒬h,ϵ\mathcal{Q}_{h,\epsilon} are finite.

Assumption 7 (Finite ϵ\epsilon-nets).

𝒩⁡(ϵ)≔maxh∈[H]⁡𝒩⁡(𝒬h,ϵ,‖⋅‖∞)<+∞\mathcal{N}(\epsilon)\coloneqq\max_{h\in[H]}\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{Q}_{h},\epsilon,\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\infty})<+\infty.

The following theorem gives the regret bound under the above more general assumptions.

Theorem 2 (Regret under general function approximation).

Suppose Assumptions 4, 5, 6, 7 hold. We let B=T​log⁡|𝒜|HB=\frac{T\log|\mathcal{A}|}{H} in Assumption 5, and set

α=(1T​H3​log⁡(𝒩⁡(ϵ/B)​H​Tδ)​dGEC​(HT))1/2.\displaystyle\alpha=\left(\frac{1}{TH^{3}\log\left(\frac{\mathcal{N}\left(\epsilon/B\right)HT}{\delta}\right)}d_{\textsf{GEC}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{H}{T}}\right)\right)^{1/2}. (116)

Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the regret of Algorithm 1 satisfies

𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝗍⁡(T)=𝒪⁡(H3/2​T​(log⁡(H​Tδ)+log⁡(𝒩⁡(H​ϵT​log⁡|𝒜|)))​dGEC​(HT)).\displaystyle\mathsf{Regret}(T)=\mathcal{O}\left(H^{3/2}\sqrt{T}\sqrt{\left(\log\left(\frac{HT}{\delta}\right)+\log\left(\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{H\epsilon}{T\log|\mathcal{A}|}\right)\right)\right)d_{\textsf{GEC}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{H}{T}}\right)}\right). (117)

Under linear MDPs, (117) reduces to (22) given in Theorem 1. Besides, this bound also matches (is slightly tighter than) the bound given in Corollary 5.2 of Liu et al. [2024] under similar assumptions.

Appendix C Value-incentivized Actor-Critic Method for Discounted MDPs

Infinite-horizon MDPs.

Let ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,P,r,γ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\gamma) be an infinite-horizon discounted MDP, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} denote the state space and the action space, respectively, γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) denotes the discount factor, P:𝒮×𝒜↦Δ⁡(𝒮)P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mapsto\Delta(\mathcal{S}) is the transition kernel, and r:𝒮×𝒜↦[0,1]r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mapsto[0,1] is the reward function. A policy π:𝒮↦Δ⁡(𝒜)\pi:\mathcal{S}\mapsto\Delta(\mathcal{A}) specifies an action selection rule, where π⁡(a|s)\pi(a|s) specifies the probability of taking action aa in state ss for each (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}. For any given policy π\pi, the value function, denoted by Vπ:𝒮↦ℝV^{\pi}:\mathcal{S}\mapsto\mathbb{R}, is given as

∀s∈𝒮:Vπ​(s)≔𝔼⁡[∑t=0∞γt​r​(st,at)|s0=s],\forall s\in\mathcal{S}:\quad V^{\pi}(s)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})|s_{0}=s\right], (151)

which measures the expected discounted cumulative reward starting from an initial state s0=ss_{0}=s, where the randomness is over the trajectory generated following at∼π(⋅|st)a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{t}) and the MDP dynamic st+1∼P(⋅|st,at)s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|s_{t},a_{t}). Given an initial state distribution s0∼ρs_{0}\sim\rho over 𝒮\mathcal{S}, we also define Vπ​(ρ)≔𝔼s∼ρ​[Vπ​(s)]V^{\pi}(\rho)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho}\left[V^{\pi}(s)\right] with slight abuse of notation. Similarly, the Q-function of policy π\pi, denoted by Qπ:𝒮×𝒜↦ℝQ^{\pi}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mapsto\mathbb{R}, is defined as

∀(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜:Qπ(s,a)≔𝔼[∑t=0∞γtr(st,at)|s0=s,a0=a],\forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}:\quad Q^{\pi}(s,a)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})|s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a\right], (152)

which measures the expected discounted cumulative reward with an initial state s0=ss_{0}=s and an initial action a0=aa_{0}=a, with expectation taken over the randomness of the trajectory. It is known that there exists at least one optimal policy π⋆\pi^{\star} that maximizes the value function Vπ​(s)V^{\pi}(s) for all states s∈𝒮s\in{\mathcal{S}} [Puterman, 2014], whose corresponding optimal value function and Q-function are denoted as V⋆V^{\star} and Q⋆Q^{\star}, respectively. We also define the state-action visitation distribution dρπ∈Δ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)d^{\pi}_{\rho}\in\Delta({\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}) induced by policy π\pi and initial state distribution ρ\rho as

dρπ​(s,a)≔(1−γ)​𝔼s0∼ρ​[∑h=0∞γh​Pr⁡(sh=s,ah=a|s0)].\displaystyle d^{\pi}_{\rho}(s,a)\coloneqq(1-\gamma)\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho}\left[\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{h}\Pr\left(s_{h}=s,a_{h}=a|s_{0}\right)\right]. (153)

C.1 Algorithm development

Similar as (13), we start with an optimization problem:

maxf∈𝒬,π\displaystyle\max_{f\in\mathcal{Q},\pi} (1−γ)𝔼s0∼ρ,a∼π(⋅|s0)[Qf(s0,a)]\displaystyle\left(1-\gamma\right)\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho,a\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{0})}\left[Q_{f}\left(s_{0},a\right)\right] (154)
s.t.\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{s.t.}}\,\, Qf(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ⋅𝔼s′∼P(⋅|s,a),a′∼π(⋅|s′)[Qf(s′,a′)],∀(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜.\displaystyle Q_{f}\left(s,a\right)=r\left(s,a\right)+\gamma\cdot\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot|s,a),a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s^{\prime})}[Q_{f}\left(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}\right)],\,\,\forall\left(s,a\right)\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}.

Writing the regularized Lagrangian system of (154) as

maxf,π(1−γ)𝔼s0∼ρ,a∼π(⋅|s0)[Qf(s0,a)]\displaystyle\max_{f,\pi}\left(1-\gamma\right)\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho,a\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{0})}\left[Q_{f}\left(s_{0},a\right)\right]
+minλ∫λ(s,a)(r(s,a)+γ⋅𝔼s′∼P(⋅|s,a),a′∼π(⋅|s′)[Qf(s′,a′)]−Qf(s,a))+β⁡(s,a)2λ(s,a)2dsda.\displaystyle+\min_{\lambda}\int\lambda(s,a)\left(r(s,a)+\gamma\cdot\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot|s,a),a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s^{\prime})}[Q_{f}\left(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}\right)]-Q_{f}\left(s,a\right)\right)+\frac{\beta(s,a)}{2}\lambda(s,a)^{2}dsda. (155)

Similar to the finite-horizon case, we use the reparameterization (10) which gives

maxf,π{(1−γ)𝔼s0∼ρ,a∼π(⋅|s0)[Qf(s0,a)]−∫12​β​(s,a)𝔼s′∼P(⋅|s,a),a′∼π(⋅|s′)[(r(s,a)+γQf(s′,a′)−Qf(s,a))2\displaystyle\max_{f,\pi}\Bigg\{(1-\gamma)\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho,a\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{0})}[Q_{f}(s_{0},a)]-\int\frac{1}{2\beta(s,a)}\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot|s,a),a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\bigg[\big(r(s,a)+\gamma Q_{f}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-Q_{f}\left(s,a\right)\big)^{2} (156)
−minρ(r(s,a)+γQf(s′,a′)−g(s,a))2]dsda},\displaystyle\hskip 18.49988pt\hskip 18.49988pt-\min_{\rho}\big(r(s,a)+\gamma Q_{f}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-g(s,a)\big)^{2}\bigg]dsda\Bigg\},

which is easier to optimize over both QfQ_{f} and π\pi. The population primal-dual optimization problem (156) prompts us to design the proposed algorithm, by computing the sample version of (156), see Algorithm 2, where we let

Vfπ(s)≔𝔼a∼π(⋅|s)[Qf(s,a)],andVfπ(ρ)≔𝔼s∼ρ[Vfπ(s)].\displaystyle V^{\pi}_{f}(s)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}\left[Q_{f}(s,a)\right],\quad\text{and}\quad V^{\pi}_{f}(\rho)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho}\left[V^{\pi}_{f}(s)\right]. (157)

In Algorithm 2, at iteration tt, given dataset 𝒟t−1\mathcal{D}_{t-1} collected from the previous iterations, we define the loss function as follows:

ℒt​(f,π)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}(f,\pi) =∑(s,a,s′)∈𝒟t−1𝔼a′∼π(⋅|s′)(r(s,a)+γQf(s′,a′)−Qf(s,a))2\displaystyle=\sum_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\in\mathcal{D}_{t-1}}\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\left(r(s,a)+\gamma Q_{f}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-Q_{f}\left(s,a\right)\right)^{2}
−infg∈𝒬∑(s,a,s′)∈𝒟t−1𝔼a′∼π(⋅|s′)(r(s,a)+γQf(s′,a′)−g(s,a))2.\displaystyle\quad\quad-\inf_{g\in\mathcal{Q}}\sum_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\in\mathcal{D}_{t-1}}\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\left(r(s,a)+\gamma Q_{f}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-g(s,a)\right)^{2}. (158)

We compute (159) in each iteration, which is the sample version of (156), and use the current policy πt\pi_{t} to collect new data following the sampling procedure in Algorithm 3, which is also used in Yuan et al. [2023, Algorithm 3], Yang et al. [2024, Algorithm 5], and Yang et al. [2025, Algorithm 7]. Algorithm 3 has an expected iteration number 𝔼⁡[h+1]=11−γ\mathbb{E}[h+1]=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}, and it guarantees ℙ⁡(sh=s,ah=a)=dρπ​(s,a)\mathbb{P}(s_{h}=s,a_{h}=a)=d^{\pi}_{\rho}(s,a) [Yuan et al., 2023] for any (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜(s,a)\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A} and any policy π\pi.

C.2 Theoretical guarantees

Same as the finite-horizon setting, we assume the following dd-dimensional linear MDP model.

Assumption 8 (infinite-horizon linear MDP).

There exists unknown vector ζ∈ℝd\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and unknown (signed) measures μ=(μ(1),⋯,μ(d))\mu=(\mu^{(1)},\cdots,\mu^{(d)}) over 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} such that

r⁡(s,a)=ϕ​(s,a)⊤​ζandP⁡(s′|s,a)=ϕ​(s,a)⊤​μ​(s′),r(s,a)=\phi(s,a)^{\top}\zeta\quad\mbox{and}\quad P(s^{\prime}|s,a)=\phi(s,a)^{\top}\mu(s^{\prime}),

where ϕ:𝒮×𝒜→ℝd\phi:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} is a known feature map satisfying ‖ϕ⁡(s,a)‖2⩽1\|\phi(s,a)\|_{2}\leqslant 1, and max⁡{‖ζ‖2,‖μ⁡(𝒮)‖2}⩽d\max\{\left\|\zeta\right\|_{2},\left\|\mu({\mathcal{S}})\right\|_{2}\}\leqslant\sqrt{d}, for all (s,a,s′)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒮(s,a,s^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times{\mathcal{S}}.

Similar as for the finite case, under Assumption 8, we only need to set the Q-function class to be linear and the policy class 𝒫\mathcal{P} to be the set of log-linear policies.

Assumption 9 (linear QQ-function class (infinite-horizon)).

The function class 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is defined as

𝒬≔{fθ≔ϕ(⋅,⋅)⊤θ:‖θ‖2⩽d1−γ,‖fθ‖∞⩽11−γ}.\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}\coloneqq\left\{f_{\theta}\coloneqq\phi(\cdot,\cdot)^{\top}\theta:\left\|\theta\right\|_{2}\leqslant\frac{\sqrt{d}}{1-\gamma},\left\|f_{\theta}\right\|_{\infty}\leqslant\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\right\}.
Assumption 10 (log-linear policy class (infinite-horizon)).

The policy class 𝒫\mathcal{P} is defined as

𝒫≔{πω:πω​(s,a)=exp⁡(ϕ​(s,a)⊤​ω)∑a′∈𝒜exp⁡(ϕ​(s,a′)⊤​ω)​with​‖ω‖2⩽B​d1−γ}\displaystyle\mathcal{P}\coloneqq\left\{\pi_{\omega}:\pi_{\omega}(s,a)=\frac{\exp\left(\phi(s,a)^{\top}\omega\right)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\exp\left(\phi(s,a^{\prime})^{\top}\omega\right)}\,\,\text{with}\,\,\left\|\omega\right\|_{2}\leqslant\frac{B\sqrt{d}}{1-\gamma}\right\}

with some constant B>0B>0.

We give the regret bound of Algorithm 2 in Theorem 3.

Theorem 3 (infinite-horizon).

Suppose Assumptions 8-10 hold. We let B=T​log⁡|𝒜|​(1−γ)dB=\frac{T\log|\mathcal{A}|(1-\gamma)}{d} in Assumption 10 and set

α=((1−γ)2T​log⁡(log⁡|𝒜|​T/δ)​log⁡(1+T3/2d​(1−γ)2))1/2.\displaystyle\alpha=\left(\frac{(1-\gamma)^{2}}{T\log\left(\log|\mathcal{A}|T/\delta\right)}\log\left(1+\frac{T^{3/2}}{d(1-\gamma)^{2}}\right)\right)^{1/2}. (160)

Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the regret of Algorithm 2 satisfies

𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝗍⁡(T)=𝒪⁡(d​T(1−γ)2​log⁡(log⁡(|𝒜|)​Tδ)​log⁡(1+T3/2d​(1−γ)2)).\displaystyle\mathsf{Regret}(T)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{d\sqrt{T}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sqrt{\log\left(\frac{\log(|\mathcal{A}|)T}{\delta}\right)\log\left(1+\frac{T^{3/2}}{d(1-\gamma)^{2}}\right)}\right). (161)

Note that

mint∈[T]⁡(V⋆​(ρ)−Vπt​(ρ))⩽𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝗍⁡(T)T,\min_{t\in[T]}\left(V^{\star}(\rho)-V^{\pi_{t}}(\rho)\right)\leqslant\frac{\mathsf{Regret}(T)}{T},

thus Theorem 3 guarantees that the iteration complexity to reach ϵ\epsilon-accuracy w.r.t. value sub-optimality for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is 𝒪~​(d2(1−γ)4​ϵ2)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{d^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{4}\epsilon^{2}}\right), and the total sample complexity is 𝒪~​(d2(1−γ)5​ϵ2)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{d^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{5}\epsilon^{2}}\right).

C.3 Proof of Theorem 3

Notation.

For notation simplicity, we let f⋆≔Q⋆f^{\star}\coloneqq Q^{\star} be the optimal Q-function. We let Π≔Δ​(𝒜)𝒮\Pi\coloneqq\Delta(\mathcal{A})^{\mathcal{S}} denote the set of all policies. We also define transition tuples

ξ≔(s,a,s′)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒮andξt≔(st,at,st′)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒮.\displaystyle\xi\coloneqq(s,a,s^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times{\mathcal{S}}\quad\text{and}\quad\xi_{t}\coloneqq(s_{t},a_{t},s^{\prime}_{t})\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times{\mathcal{S}}. (162)

Given any policy π\pi and f:𝒮×𝒜→ℝf:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, we define ℙπ​f\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f as

∀(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜:ℙπf(s,a)≔r(s,a)+γ𝔼s′∼ℙ(⋅|s,a),a′∼π(⋅|s′)[f(s′,a′)].\displaystyle\forall(s,a)\in{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}:\quad\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f(s,a)\coloneqq r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim\mathbb{P}(\cdot|s,a),a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\left[f(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right]. (163)

We let

Θ≔{θ:fθ∈𝒬},Ω≔{ω:‖ω‖2⩽B​d1−γ}\displaystyle\Theta\coloneqq\{\theta:f_{\theta}\in\mathcal{Q}\},\quad\Omega\coloneqq\left\{\omega:\left\|\omega\right\|_{2}\leqslant\frac{B\sqrt{d}}{1-\gamma}\right\} (164)

be the parameter space of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and 𝒫\mathcal{P}, respectively.

We’ll repeatedly use the following lemma, which is a standard consequence of linear MDP.

Lemma 12 (Linear MDP ⇒\Rightarrow Bellman completeness + realizability (infinite-horizon)).

Under Assumption 8, we have

  • •

    (realizability) Q⋆∈𝒬Q^{\star}\in\mathcal{Q};

  • •

    (Bellman completeness) ∀π∈Π\forall\pi\in\Pi and f∈𝒬f\in\mathcal{Q}, ℙπ​f∈𝒬\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f\in\mathcal{Q}.

We’ll also use the following lemma, which bounds the difference between the optimal value function V⋆​(ρ)V^{\star}(\rho) and maxπ∈𝒫⁡Vπ​(ρ)\max_{\pi\in\mathcal{P}}V^{\pi}(\rho) — the optimal value over the policy class 𝒫\mathcal{P}, where we let

π~⋆≔arg⁡maxπ∈𝒫​Vf⋆π​(ρ).\displaystyle\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}\coloneqq\arg\max_{\pi\in\mathcal{P}}V_{f^{\star}}^{\pi}(\rho). (165)
Lemma 13 (model error with log linear policies (infinite-horizon)).

Under Assumptions 8-10, we have

∀s∈𝒮:0⩽V⋆​(s)−Vf⋆π~⋆​(s)⩽log⁡|𝒜|B,\displaystyle\forall s\in{\mathcal{S}}:\quad 0\leqslant V^{\star}(s)-V_{f^{\star}}^{\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}}(s)\leqslant\frac{\log|\mathcal{A}|}{B}, (166)

where BB is defined in Assumption 10.

We omit the proofs of the above two lemmas due to similarity to that of the finite-horizon setting.

Main proof of Theorem 3.

Given the regret decomposition in (29), we will bound the two terms separately.

Step 1: bounding term (i).

C.4 Proof of key lemmas

C.4.1 Proof of Lemma 14

We bound the two terms ℒt​(f⋆,π~⋆)\mathcal{L}_{t}(f^{\star},\widetilde{\pi}^{\star}) and −ℒt​(ft,πt)-\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{t},\pi_{t}) in the left-hand side of (169) separately. Given f,f′:𝒮×𝒜→ℝf,f^{\prime}:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, data tuple ξ=(s,a,s′)\xi=(s,a,s^{\prime}) and policy π\pi, we define the random variable

l⁡(f,f′,ξ,π)≔r⁡(s,a)+γ​f​(s′,a′)−f′​(s,a),\displaystyle l(f,f^{\prime},\xi,\pi)\coloneqq r(s,a)+\gamma f(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-f^{\prime}(s,a), (176)

l⁡(f,ℙπ​f,ξ,π)=γ⁡(f⁡(s′,a′)−𝔼s′∼ℙ(⋅|s,a)a′∼π(⋅|s′)​[f⁡(s′,a′)]).\displaystyle l(f,\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f,\xi,\pi)=\gamma\Big(f(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim\mathbb{P}(\cdot|s,a)\atop a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\left[f(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right]\Big). (177)

Combining (176) and (177), we deduce that for any f,f′:𝒮×𝒜→ℝf,f^{\prime}:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, ξ\xi and π\pi,

l⁡(f,f′,ξ,π)−l⁡(f,ℙπ​f,ξ,π)=𝔼s′∼ℙ(⋅|s,a)a′∼π(⋅|s′)​[l⁡(f,f′,ξ,π)].\displaystyle l(f,f^{\prime},\xi,\pi)-l(f,\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f,\xi,\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim\mathbb{P}(\cdot|s,a)\atop a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\left[l(f,f^{\prime},\xi,\pi)\right]. (178)
Bounding −ℒt​(ft,πt)-\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{t},\pi_{t}).

For any f∈𝒬,πf\in\mathcal{Q},\pi and t∈[T]t\in[T], we define Xf,πtX_{f,\pi}^{t} as

Xf,πt≔𝔼a′∼π(⋅|st′)[l(f,f,ξt,π)2−l(f,ℙπf,ξt,π)2].\displaystyle X_{f,\pi}^{t}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{t}^{\prime})}\left[l(f,f,\xi_{t},\pi)^{2}-l(f,\mathbb{P}^{\pi}f,\xi_{t},\pi)^{2}\right]. (179)

Then we have for any f∈𝒬f\in\mathcal{Q}:

Below we use Freedman’s inequality (Lemma 1) and a covering number argument to give the desired bound. where we define
